summary:
Baja California Sur records no legal hostility toward trans visitors. The state Congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure through a reform of the state Civil Code in 2021, and the sources reviewed document no criminalisation of trans presence or of gender expression in the state.

Recognition has widened rather than narrowed. After Mexico's Supreme Court ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from the procedure was unconstitutional, the state Congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending legal gender recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people. El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform allows minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, with the administrative processes described as rapid, free and free of prejudice; the XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court ruling.

The national framework around the state is uneven. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's 32 states operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Physical risk follows the national baseline rather than any documented local pattern. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights warned in 2024 that impunity may have reached alarming levels while pressing federal and state authorities to prevent and punish violence against trans people.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
tangentialFactors:
Comparison with a non-reforming state frames the Baja California Sur position. Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that Tabasco, which has no legal gender recognition procedure, exposes trans residents to institutional mistreatment: the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling their legal names. Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition there leave trans people carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" on 18 July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with sentences of up to 70 years, in one of the deadliest settings for trans people in the hemisphere. The statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
localsOnly:
The recognition procedure is resident-facing civil-registry machinery. The 2021 Civil Code reform established an administrative route to legal gender recognition, and the 2024 reform extended it to children, adolescents and non-binary people, allowing minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates through processes the state congress described as rapid, free and free of prejudice.

Residents elsewhere in Mexico face a different administrative picture. In Tabasco, delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling their legal names.

Partnership rights are settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
outOfScopeNotes:
No incident of violence against a trans person in Baja California Sur, and no enforcement pattern specific to the state, appears in the sources reviewed. How the state's authorities investigate and punish killings of trans people remains unresolved in this material.

Whether the Baja California Sur criminal code contains hate-motivation provisions covering anti-trans violence is not sourced here. The transfemicide statute documented in the inventory is the one approved by Mexico City's Congress on 18 July 2024, and its application in Baja California Sur is not established.

Implementation of the 2024 Civil Code reform is documented only up to the point of approval; processing times, refusals and appeal routes for applicants in the state are not sourced. Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans visitors fall outside the material reviewed.
